facts.claim: "Empty House" was released as a single on March 24, 2024, on the label The Gringos.
The song runs 4:27 and is a one-track single.
Shazam credits the writing of "Empty House" to Jacob Reina and Pat McNeill.
Deezer lists Jacob Reina as writer. Its composer credits are Jacob Reina, Patrick McNeill, Connor Grimes, Andrew William Lancaster and Raymond Mann.
The YouTube release credits Jacob Reina on lead vocals and list electric guitar. The listing is truncated, and its copyright line reads ℗ 2023 The Gringos LLC.
The Gringos are from Athens, Georgia.
The Gringos are a five-piece indie rock band of University of Georgia students. Singer Jacob Reina and guitarist Raymond Mann were interviewed ahead of the band's first SXSW appearance.
Reina says he writes most of the band's lyrics and guitarist Pat McNeill writes some.
"Empty House" has been performed live. It appears in a setlist from a show at Workplay in Birmingham, AL, alongside "Tossing and Turning", "Strange" and "In Retro".
After "Empty House", the band's singles include "In Retro" and "Fading" (2025), "Keepin' The Road" (2025) and "Strange" (2026).

research.lineage: The Gringos are an Athens, Georgia college-band indie rock group playing loose, melodic rock, and Shazam tags the song as indie rock and college rock.

draft:
Nobody sings harmony on **Empty House**. For a song with that title, the choice carries weight. Jacob Reina's voice comes in clear and mid-range, smooth and melodic, and it stays on its own. No second voice comes in to keep it company. In a song named for a place where people used to be, a voice left alone in the mix does a lot of the emotional work before you could name a single line.

The Gringos are a five-piece out of Athens, Georgia, a band of University of Georgia students, and this is college rock in the plain sense of the tag: melodic, unfussy, built by friends who clearly listen to each other. Reina, who says he writes most of the band's lyrics, shares the writing credit here with guitarist Pat McNeill. That two-person core shows in how the song is put together. Nothing is there for show.

Start with the guitars. An acoustic is fingerpicked in a rolling arpeggio, steady as a clock in a quiet room. Over it, an electric guitar holds long, clean, sustained notes that hang rather than move. The two set up a gentle tension: one keeps time, the other lingers. The bass plays a simple, foundational line, and the drums are brushed, slow and steady. That choice keeps the floor soft under everything, so the song never pushes forward. It sways in place.

The production is clean and polished, with each instrument clearly separated. The room sounds medium-sized, with a little air around the players. That openness matters. A house only sounds empty when you can hear the space around the sound, and here you can.

What the song holds is a kind of stillness that isn't peace. The relaxed tempo and the brushed drums say calm. The lone voice and those suspended electric notes say something is missing. The band doesn't settle which one is true. The arrangement keeps its restraint, and the restraint reads less like a style and more like care, the way people talk quietly in a room after someone has left it.

It's a young band's song, and it doesn't reach for size. It has found a stage beyond the dorm room, though. The Gringos have played it live, including a set at Workplay in Birmingham alongside "Strange" and "In Retro." Later singles like "Fading" and "Keepin' The Road" followed it. But this one is a good place to meet them: modest, patient, and sure of its mood.

The song sticks because it makes a quiet room sound full of something, and it leaves you to sit in that absence instead of hurrying you past it.
